meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
I know who you are, Hale. Who decided on the zero, and did anyone speak to Owen first?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.

Pretty conclusive. Turnitin's own guide says its indicator shouldn't be the sole basis for punishing a student, and your school's procedure says software alone doesn't establish anything. What else do you have?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Now show me what you have on the essay itself.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing down 11:52 and 11:58. Owen told me he wrote it over the weekend, so he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in. That's what this shows.

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Turn it toward me. Students misquote all the time, Hale; a wrong line from a study guide is a mistake, not proof of anything.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
He changed his thesis in two weeks. That's what an outline is for, Hale.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.
A five-minute quiz after class isn't a hearing, and a September in-class piece is not a weekend essay. I want copies of those notes and the 3.2 page tonight. So what exactly are you proposing?

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
Then 4.4, in writing tonight, with nothing on his file. He'll do the rewrite to put this behind him, not because he did anything, and it gets marked before December 1. When?
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday the 12th, after school, private, and the mark entered well before December 1. I'll want all of that in your email tonight.
Do we have an agreement?
We do, once it's in writing tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

In our meeting today you agreed that Owen will do a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes under procedure 4.4 after school on Thursday, November 12, that its mark will replace the zero and be entered well before December 1, and that nothing will go on his record. I still require that agreement in writing, along with copies of your November 2 notes and the page of Act 3, Scene 2 you showed me. I expect it in writing tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: She reached her last position and agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, but she still wants the agreement in writing tonight, nothing on Owen's record, and copies of your notes and the play page, and that is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, reached before her time ran out.
What moved her: You offered procedure 4.4 in writing with nothing on his record after you had shown your evidence, which met the one demand she would never give up.
What cost ground: You opened with the checker score and called it conclusive, which gave her the weakest piece of your case to attack first.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history put the essay appearing in large blocks just before midnight on October 28, the night before it was due, which came very close to that kind of late October night; it proves nothing about the essay, but it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she said the invented Hamlet line could have come from a study guide, answer that point directly before moving on to the outline, so the strongest checkable piece stands on its own.
